items.question: what is aurora in this ui mean
items.answer:
"Aurora" is just the name of this design for DevDeck, not a feature or a tool. It shows up in a few places:

- **The small "Aurora" badge next to the DevDeck logo.** It's a leftover label from when this design was built as a new version alongside an older sidebar design. The older design was later removed, so the badge no longer tells you anything useful.
- **The "Aurora Neon" theme.** It's one of the colour choices in the Theme menu: purple and cyan with soft glowing colours drifting in the background, like the northern lights. The default theme is High Contrast, and Aurora Neon is the original look.
- **Old links.** Addresses that start with `/aurora/…` were this design's first home, and they still open the right page.
- **Behind the scenes,** your saved settings (theme, pinned tools, recent tools) are stored under names that start with "aurora". You never see this.

Since the badge is confusing, I'd remove it from the top bar. I can also rename the "Aurora Neon" theme if you'd like a plainer name, and your saved settings and old links would keep working either way. Want me to do that?

items.question: i want to made it support the thirt party plugin or can add new tool funtion if i input any github repo can it possible
items.answer:
Yes, this is possible. The catch is that a tool added from GitHub would be someone else's code running inside DevDeck, so it needs safety limits. It also can't work with any repo: DevDeck can only add tools from repos written as DevDeck plugins.

**How it could work**
1. In Settings → Manage tools, you paste a GitHub repo address, such as `github.com/someone/devdeck-base32`.
2. DevDeck reads a small description file in that repo. It says the tool's name, its group, and what kind of tool it is.
3. Before installing, DevDeck shows what the tool is and where it came from, and asks you to confirm.
4. The tool then appears in a "Plugins" group and in search, like a built-in tool. You can switch it off or remove it in Manage tools.

**Keeping it safe**
- **Sealed box.** Each plugin runs in a sealed-off box inside the page. It gets only the text you give it and sends back a result. It can't see your other tools, your saved settings, or anything else you type, and it can't reach the internet unless you allow it.
- **Pinned version.** DevDeck keeps the exact version you approved, so a later change in the repo can't quietly alter the tool.
- **Simple tools only.** "Text in, result out" tools work well this way: encoders, converters, formatters, checkers, generators. Plugins that need their own complex screens are much harder to do safely.

**What wouldn't work**
- A random project on GitHub: DevDeck wouldn't know how to turn it into a tool.
- Private repos.
- Plugins that sync between devices: they'd be saved in each browser separately.

**Smaller options**
- **No-code tools.** Build a new tool from existing DevDeck steps, using Tool Chain. For example: "Base64 decode → format JSON → sort keys", saved under its own name, with its own page and search entry. No outside code, so no risk.
- **Built in by the owner.** The site owner adds a plugin repo to the project and rebuilds. Safe, but visitors can't add their own.

**My recommendation**
Start with the sealed-box plugins, plus a template repo that shows how to write one. Add the no-code tools too, since they're quick and risk-free. I haven't changed anything yet. If you'd like this, say "add plugin support from GitHub repos" (or "start with no-code custom tools") and I'll build it.

items.question: help me think about the current commit message
items.answer:
I'll check what's in git right now before suggesting anything.I can't open any files this session, so I can't see whether you've already started a message. If you have one, paste it here and I'll go over it. Here's how I'd approach it from what I know of the project.

**This will probably be the first commit.** When I started, the project had no commits yet and every file was new. So the message should describe the whole project, not just the last fix (the Pin star). A message like "fix pin button" would mislead anyone reading the history later.

**A suggested message:**

```
Initial commit: DevDeck — 73 developer tools that run in the browser

- Tools grouped by task: Convert, Encode/Decode, Format, Generate,
  Validate, Calculate, Text, JSON & XML, Network, Files & Images, Reference
- Smart Paste, Tool Chain, quick search (Ctrl/⌘ K), pins and recent tools
- Themes and layout presets (Modern web, Compact, Desktop app, …),
  tool sets (Essentials / Standard / Complete)
- Works on phones and tablets, can be added to the home screen,
  works offline, link-preview thumbnails
- Command-line version: npm run cli
```

The first line is the part most tools show, so keep it short and say what the project is. The list underneath is for someone who wants more detail.

**Before committing:** some folders shouldn't go into the commit at all.
- **`node_modules`** is downloaded libraries, rebuilt by `npm install`.
- **`dist`** is the built site, rebuilt by `npm run build`.
- **Craft Anything's own records** (`craft.json`, `feed.json`, `questions.json`, `usage.json`, `build-activity.log`, `inbox`, `capture`, `investigation.cany`) are working notes, not part of DevDeck.

To leave these out, add a `.gitignore` file that lists them. If you want, ask me to add it in your next build request; it's a one-line change per item.

If this isn't the first commit, tell me what changed since the last one, and I'll write a shorter message that covers just that.
